items.stem: What best distinguishes a modular monolith from a layered (N-tier) application?

options.text: Modules are vertical slices of business capability with enforced boundaries, deployed as one unit
options.rationale: Correct: a modular monolith partitions by capability with enforced boundaries while still deploying as a single unit.

options.text: Each module is deployed as a separate process behind a load balancer
options.rationale: That describes microservices, not a modular monolith, which deploys as one unit.

options.text: Layers (UI, business, data) are the modules
options.rationale: Horizontal technical layers are not capability modules; that is the N-tier style being contrasted.

options.text: It forbids any shared code between modules
options.rationale: A shared kernel of common code is allowed; the rule is no reaching into another module internals.

items.explanation: Correct: a modular monolith partitions by capability with enforced boundaries while still deploying as a single unit.

items.stem: You must keep modules decoupled in a .NET modular monolith. Select TWO practices that preserve module boundaries.

options.text: Expose a public contract (interface + DTO) and keep entities module-private
options.rationale: Correct: a narrow public contract hides internals and keeps modules decoupled.

options.text: Communicate between modules through an in-process mediator message
options.rationale: Correct: in-process messaging avoids direct dependencies on another module internal types.

options.text: Share one EF Core DbContext across all modules for convenience
options.rationale: A shared DbContext couples modules at the data layer and breaks boundaries.

options.text: Let the Billing module call Ordering internal repository classes directly
options.rationale: Calling internal classes across modules is exactly the coupling boundaries are meant to prevent.

options.text: Reference another module concrete entity types from controllers
options.rationale: Depending on another module concrete types leaks internals and couples the modules.

items.explanation: Correct: a narrow public contract hides internals and keeps modules decoupled.

items.stem: A team is under no scaling or organizational pressure but wants to "future-proof" by splitting the monolith into microservices now. What is the most appropriate guidance?

options.text: Stay a modular monolith and extract a service only when a concrete driver appears
options.rationale: Correct: premature extraction adds distributed-systems complexity with little benefit until a real driver exists.

options.text: Split immediately so the architecture is never a bottleneck
options.rationale: Early splitting adds network, consistency and operational cost without a justifying need.

options.text: Convert every module into its own database first
options.rationale: Separate databases add distributed-data complexity and are not required for a modular monolith.

options.text: Remove module boundaries to simplify the future split
options.rationale: Removing boundaries makes a future split harder, not easier.

items.explanation: Correct: premature extraction adds distributed-systems complexity with little benefit until a real driver exists.
